Dissension means strong disagreement among people within the same group — disagreement serious enough to cause tension, conflict, or division between them.

Think of it this way: when people who are supposed to be on the same side start clashing, arguing, and pulling in different directions, that friction and internal conflict is called dissension.

There are two things that make dissension special and different from just any ordinary disagreement:

1. It happens inside a group.
Dissension is almost always internal. It's not about two rival companies fighting each other, or two countries going to war. It's about cracks forming within — inside a political party, inside a family, inside a team, inside a company, inside a government. The people disagreeing are supposed to be united under one common roof, but they're not.

2. It's serious and divisive, not just mild.
Dissension isn't two friends having a small debate about which movie to watch. It's the kind of disagreement that breaks things apart — that makes people take sides, lose trust in each other, and stops a group from functioning well. It has a deeply negative and destructive quality.

• "Dissension within the ruling party made it impossible to pass any new laws."

Here, members of the same political party are fighting among themselves, making the whole party weak.

  • "The question of how to divide their late father's property caused bitter dissension among the four siblings."

A family torn apart from the inside by a serious disagreement.

  • "The coach worried that dissension in the team would cost them the championship."

Players arguing and taking sides against each other, destroying team unity.

  • "Years of dissension had left the organization fractured and leaderless."

Long-running internal conflict slowly destroyed a group.

Dissension carries a negative tone. When you use this word, you are signalling that something is wrong — that a group is unhealthy, unstable, or in trouble. It suggests things are not just tense but actively breaking down. Writers and speakers often use it to describe situations that are alarming or serious.
Dissension vs. Words That Feel Similar

Understanding how dissension differs from related words will sharpen your grasp of it significantly.

Dissension vs. Disagreement
A disagreement can be small, polite, and harmless — two colleagues calmly holding different opinions. Dissension is bigger, more heated, and damaging. All dissension involves disagreement, but not all disagreement rises to the level of dissension.

Dissension vs. Dissent
Dissent refers to one person (or a smaller group) openly opposing the majority or those in authority. It is the act of saying "I disagree with what everyone else has decided." Dissension is the broader state of conflict and division that results when multiple disagreements are tearing a group apart. Dissent is more like a single voice of opposition; dissension is the whole storm of internal conflict.

Dissension vs. Discord
Discord means a general lack of harmony — friction and bad feeling between people. It's a slightly broader and vaguer word. Dissension is more specific: it always points to disagreement as the root cause of that friction.

Dissension vs. Conflict
Conflict is a very broad word — it covers any kind of struggle, fight, or clash, including wars between nations or physical fights. Dissension is specifically verbal and ideological — it's about people disagreeing in their minds, opinions, and positions. And again, it's always internal to a group.

Dissension sits in the upper-middle range of disagreement. It's more serious than a "difference of opinion" or a "debate," but it doesn't necessarily mean people are physically fighting. Think of it as the point where disagreement has grown so strong that it is clearly harming the group — but the people may still be sitting in the same room or organization, just deeply divided.

These are the most natural ways you will see and hear dissension used:

  • "Sow dissension" — To deliberately create disagreement and division in a group. "The spy's job was to sow dissension among the enemy's allies." (Sow = to plant seeds of something.)
  • "Internal dissension" — Emphasizes that the conflict is from within.
  • "Dissension in the ranks" — A classic phrase meaning disagreement among the members or lower levels of an organization, especially a military or political one.
  • "Dissension among [a group]" — "There is growing dissension among the board members."
  • "Cause / create / stir up dissension"

Dissension is a moderately formal word. You will see it most often in news articles, political writing, historical accounts, and professional contexts. In everyday casual conversation, people are more likely to say things like "they're fighting among themselves" or "there's a lot of conflict in that group." But when you want to sound precise, informed, and serious — particularly in writing — dissension is exactly the right word.

Dissension is the serious, damaging conflict and division that arises from strong disagreement among people within the same group.

Master that, and you've mastered the word.
